title: The First Emperor: How Qin Unified China

scenes.purpose: Hook: the discovery of the clay army and the man it was built for.

visual.title: The man who made China
visual.statement: In 221 BC, one king conquered his rivals and declared himself the First Emperor.

narration.text: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an struck pieces of a life-sized clay figure.
It belonged to an army of thousands, buried for more than two thousand years.
The army was made for one man: the First Emperor of China.
He united seven warring kingdoms,
forced them to share one set of standards,
and prepared to keep ruling even after death.

scenes.purpose: Set the long era of war in time.

visual.title: Two and a half centuries of war

events.label: Ying Zheng becomes king of Qin

narration.text: For more than two centuries, China was a battlefield.
Historians call this the Warring States period, starting around 475 BC.
In 356 BC, the state of Qin began reforms that turned it into a war machine.
In 246 BC, a boy named Ying Zheng became king of Qin, at about thirteen.
Twenty-five years later, he would rule all of China.

scenes.purpose: Describe the seven kingdoms and how they fought.

visual.title: Seven kingdoms, one prize
visual.statement: Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei fought for control of the Chinese heartland.

narration.text: By then, seven large kingdoms had swallowed their smaller neighbors.
Their armies grew to hundreds of thousands of foot soldiers.
Iron weapons and crossbows made battles deadlier than ever.
And alliances shifted constantly, as the others ganged up on whoever seemed strongest.

scenes.purpose: Show the scale of the fighting, with caution about ancient numbers.

visual.title: War on a staggering scale

stats.label: soldiers said to have died at Changping, 260 BC

visual.note: The Changping figure comes from ancient histories; modern scholars think it is inflated.

narration.text: The era lasted about two hundred and fifty years.
At the battle of Changping in 260 BC, ancient accounts claim Qin killed four hundred thousand enemy soldiers.
Modern historians think that number is exaggerated, but the slaughter was real.

scenes.purpose: Explain why Qin became strongest.

visual.title: Why Qin won
visual.statement: Qin rebuilt itself as a disciplined war machine, run on strict laws and rewards for merit.

narration.text: Why did Qin, a rough frontier state in the west, come out on top?
Its reformer, Shang Yang, rewarded soldiers with land and rank for success in battle.
Harsh laws applied to everyone, and neighbors were made to report each other's crimes.
Farming and fighting were the respected jobs; merchants and scholars ranked low.

scenes.purpose: Define Legalism.

visual.title: The philosophy behind Qin
visual.definition: The belief that clear laws, harsh punishments and generous rewards, not virtue, keep a state strong.
visual.example: Its ideas guided the king's chief minister, Li Si.

narration.text: This approach was later called Legalism.
Legalists believed that clear laws, harsh punishments and generous rewards, not moral virtue, kept a state strong.
Its ideas guided the king's chief minister, Li Si.

scenes.purpose: Show the conquest of the six rival kingdoms in order.

narration.text: From his base in the west, King Zheng began to swallow his rivals one by one.
Han fell first, in 230 BC.
Zhao followed in 228,
Wei in 225,
and the vast southern kingdom of Chu in 223.
Yan fell in 222,
and in 221 BC, Qi surrendered almost without a fight.

scenes.purpose: Explain the new imperial title.

visual.title: The First Emperor
visual.statement: He took a brand-new title, Shi Huangdi, and expected his dynasty to rule for ten thousand generations.

narration.text: In 221 BC, King Zheng ruled all of China.
No old title seemed grand enough, so he invented one: Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor.
His heirs, he declared, would be the Second Emperor, the Third, and so on for ten thousand generations.
His dynasty would last just fifteen years.

scenes.purpose: Introduce standardization as the key to unity.

visual.title: One empire, one standard
visual.statement: To hold a huge and varied land together, the emperor made everything uniform.
points: One set of weights and measures

narration.text: Conquering China was one thing; holding it together was another.
The emperor's answer was standardization.
Across the empire, officials now wrote in one script,
paid in one round bronze coin with a square hole,
and used one set of weights and measures.

scenes.purpose: Contrast the patchwork before unification with the standards after.

narration.text: Before unification, each kingdom wrote many characters its own way, and minted its own coins.
Even cart axles came in different widths, so wheels did not fit the ruts of foreign roads.
Afterward, one script, one coin and one axle width ran from one end of the empire to the other.

scenes.purpose: Show how the empire was governed.

narration.text: The emperor also swept away the old hereditary lords.
Power now flowed down from the emperor,
through thirty-six commanderies, each run by appointed officials,
down to counties,
and finally to every village household.
Officials were chosen, paid and replaced by the court, not born into power.

scenes.purpose: Describe the roads, canals and relay stations.

visual.title: Roads, canals and couriers
visual.statement: Imperial roads and canals let armies, officials and orders move fast across the empire.

narration.text: To move armies and orders quickly, the empire built roads and canals.
The Straight Road ran some seven hundred kilometers north from the capital to the frontier.
In the south, the Lingqu Canal linked the river systems of the Yangtze and the Pearl.
And relay stations passed messages along the roads at speed.

scenes.purpose: Separate the Qin wall from the Ming wall tourists see.

narration.text: The emperor is also linked to the Great Wall, but the story is more complicated.
His general Meng Tian joined older walls into a long northern barrier, mostly of rammed earth.
Most of that wall has long since worn away.
The brick wall tourists visit today was built much later, under the Ming dynasty.

scenes.purpose: Show the human cost of the wall.

visual.title: Building the northern wall

stats.label: men sent north with General Meng Tian
the wall's traditional length, about 5,000 km

visual.note: Both figures come from ancient histories and tradition.

narration.text: Ancient histories say three hundred thousand men were sent north to fight and to build.
The wall's traditional name means the wall of ten thousand li, roughly five thousand kilometers.
Countless workers died, and folk tales mourned them for centuries.

scenes.purpose: Tell the story of the burning of the books, with its uncertainties.

visual.title: Silencing the critics
visual.statement: In 213 BC, the government ordered old histories and many works of philosophy burned.

narration.text: Unity also meant controlling ideas.
In 213 BC, on Li Si's advice, the emperor ordered the histories of the other states and many philosophy books burned.
Books on medicine, farming and fortune-telling were spared.
According to a later Han historian, hundreds of scholars were then put to death.
Historians still debate how much of this is true, but it shaped his reputation for two thousand years.

scenes.purpose: Describe the emperor's fear of death.

visual.title: Afraid to die
visual.statement: The most powerful man in China spent his last years trying to cheat death.

narration.text: For all his power, the emperor feared one thing above all: death.
He sought elixirs of immortality from magicians and alchemists.
He sent expeditions out to sea to find the islands of the immortals.
And he toured his empire, climbing sacred mountains to perform rituals.

scenes.purpose: Show how quickly the dynasty collapsed after his death.

narration.text: In 210 BC, he died while touring the eastern provinces.
Some historians suspect the mercury in his potions hastened his end.
The old histories say his ministers hid the death, masking the smell with a cart of salted fish.
Within a year, revolts broke out across the empire.
By 206 BC, the Qin dynasty was gone,
and by 202 BC, the Han dynasty had taken its place, keeping much of the Qin system.

scenes.purpose: Locate the tomb and the clay army.

narration.text: The emperor's tomb lies east of his old capital, Xianyang, close to the modern city of Xi'an.
About a kilometer and a half east of the burial mound, the farmers found the clay army.
Archaeologists have been digging there ever since.

scenes.purpose: Give the size of the terracotta army.

visual.title: An army for the afterlife
visual.note: Estimates for the three main pits; most figures are still underground.

narration.text: Archaeologists estimate the pits hold about eight thousand soldiers,
around one hundred thirty chariots,
and some six hundred seventy horses.
Most of them have not yet been dug up.

scenes.purpose: Explain how the warriors were made.

narration.text: The figures were made almost on a production line.
Workers pressed legs, bodies and arms from molds,
then finished each head by hand, so the faces look strikingly individual.
The figures were fired in kilns,
then painted in bright colors, most of which flaked away soon after excavation.

scenes.purpose: Describe the unopened tomb.

visual.title: The tomb no one has opened
visual.statement: The emperor's burial mound has never been excavated, and for now it will stay sealed.

narration.text: And the emperor's own tomb has never been opened.
A Han historian wrote that it held rivers of flowing mercury.
Remarkably, soil tests over the mound have found unusually high levels of mercury.
The same account warns of crossbows rigged to shoot intruders.
For now, China has chosen to leave it sealed, until it can be excavated without damage.

scenes.purpose: Explain the lasting legacy of Qin.

visual.title: A blueprint for two thousand years
visual.statement: The Qin dynasty lasted fifteen years, but its system shaped Chinese government for two millennia.

narration.text: The First Emperor's dynasty barely outlived him.
But a shared script let people with very different dialects read the same texts for centuries.
Rule by appointed officials became the model for the dynasties that followed.
And many scholars think the word China itself may come from the name Qin.

scenes.purpose: Close by weighing his two faces.

narration.text: So was he a visionary builder or a ruthless tyrant?
He ended centuries of war and laid the framework of a civilization.
But he did it with brutal laws, forced labor and the silencing of critics.
More than two thousand years later, China still lives with both sides of his legacy.
